text: Psalm 91 opens with the word "sit." Protection begins with resting in a finished work.
explanation:
"He who dwells in the secret place of the Most High" begins in Hebrew with yashab: he who sits. In Hebrew, the first word usually carries the emphasis. The Old Testament priests always stood; the tabernacle had a table but no chair, because their work was never done. But Jesus, "after He had offered one sacrifice for sins forever, sat down at the right hand of God," and you are seated with Him.

When the enemy asks, "What are you going to do about this?" you can say, "Nothing. It's done." Before you get up each morning, lie there and tell yourself, "I'm seated with Christ. It's finished." The things that trouble you are always things not yet done. In Him, they're settled.

text: Psalm 91 begins and ends with the Hebrew letter for "hand." You're held in both of His.
explanation:
The very first letter of Psalm 91 is yod, the hand. The very last letter of its final word is yod too. Every promise in between, from the feathers that cover you to the long life that satisfies you, sits between two hands.

Jesus said, "No one shall snatch them out of My hand… no one is able to snatch them out of My Father's hand." A one-handed grip can slip; two hands make an embrace. That's how you're held.

text: "Peace be with you; do not fear, you shall not die." The first time God reveals Himself as the Lord our Peace, it's with these words.
explanation:
Gideon realised he'd seen the Angel of the Lord face to face and thought he would die. "Then the Lord said to him, 'Peace be with you; do not fear, you shall not die.'" Gideon built an altar and called it Jehovah Shalom, the Lord is Peace. It's the first time that name appears, and it's tied to deliverance from death.

Paul uses the same title: "The God of peace will crush Satan under your feet shortly." During the SARS outbreak, this was the word given to a congregation of about 8,000, and none of its regular attendees died. Receive it for yourself and your family: peace be to you. Do not fear. You shall not die.

text: Gideon said, "Where are all His miracles?" God answered, "Go in this might of yours."
explanation:
Gideon was threshing wheat in hiding, afraid of the Midianites, full of questions: "If the Lord is with us, why then has all this happened to us?" That doesn't sound like strong faith. Yet the Lord turned to him and said, "Go in this might of yours… Have I not sent you?"

What might? His weakness. In God's hands, the very weakness you're embarrassed by becomes the opportunity for His strength. "My clan is the weakest… and I am the least," Gideon protested. "Surely I will be with you," the Lord replied. That's all the might you need.

text: "The Lord will pass over the door and not allow the destroyer to come into your houses."
explanation:
Read quickly, the Passover story sounds as if God Himself sends the plague. But a few verses later, a third party appears: the Lord "will not allow the destroyer to come into your houses to strike you." Hebrew often speaks of God doing what He permits. His hand has been holding back destruction all along, far more than we realise.

The one thing that kept Israel safe was the blood on the doorposts and lintel, a picture of the cross. Don't take it for granted. Cover yourself and your family with the blood of Jesus every day. Where He sees the blood, the destroyer isn't permitted in.

text: In Hebrew, "pestilence" (deber) and "word" (dabar) share the same letters. What you say matters.
explanation:
Deber, the pestilence of Psalm 91, is spelled with exactly the same three letters as dabar, word; only the vowel points differ. And look at how the psalm turns: "I will say of the Lord, 'He is my refuge and my fortress'… Surely He shall deliver you… from the perilous pestilence."

You don't live by the law of averages: it might be me, it might not. "Death and life are in the power of the tongue." Don't say "I'm dying for that"; say what God says. "You shall not be afraid… of the pestilence that walks in darkness." Speak His word over your home.

text: Planes don't abolish gravity; a higher law lifts them above it. That's how the law of the Spirit of life works in you.
explanation:
"For the law of the Spirit of life in Christ Jesus has made me free from the law of sin and death." Grey hair, wrinkles, weariness and disease come from the law of sin and death that entered through Adam. That law is still real, like gravity. But every day at the airport, aircraft rise above gravity because a stronger law, lift, is at work.

During a bubonic plague in Africa, the missionary John G. Lake buried the dead for months without falling ill. When a doctor asked what precautions he took, he pointed to this verse. He taught that fear makes you absorb what's around you, while faith repels it. You're under a higher law. Rest in it.
